messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Threat → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Marlene is a 69-year-old woman who has worked as an agricultural laborer for over four decades, picking fruit and vegetables across the Central Valley. She is married and lives with her husband in a small mobile home on the edge of a farming community. She came to therapy at the urging of her daughter, who noticed that Marlene had stopped visiting, stopped answering the phone, and had become thin and hollow-eyed. Marlene reported a PCL-5 score of 67, and what emerged over the first sessions was a story that began nearly two years ago, when she was assaulted by a supervisor in the back of a company truck after a long shift. It happened at dusk, in the dirt lot behind the packing shed, and she had not told anyone until now. She had been certain, she said, that no one would believe her, and that she would be blamed.

In the months that followed, Marlene found that a memory of the event would come to her without warning—the smell of diesel and dust, the weight of the man’s hand over her mouth. These intrusive memories were most likely to surface when she was riding the bus to work, the lurch and stop of the vehicle pulling her back to the truck bed, or when certain conversation topics arose among coworkers: jokes about the supervisor, talk about overtime, any mention of the packing shed. The memories made her feel as though she was back there, and she would become flooded with fear and shame so intense that she felt she might break apart. To cope, she began drinking a few beers after work, and then more, and she started mentally rehearsing worst-case scenarios before every shift—imagining the supervisor cornering her again, imagining what she would do, how she would scream, where she would run. She told herself that if she prepared for the worst, she would not be caught off guard again.

But the rehearsals only made the memories come more often. The more she imagined the worst, the more the real memory intruded, vivid and fresh. And the drinking, she noticed, made her drowsy and careless the next day, which meant she was less alert, and then the memories would hit her harder, without warning. She began to avoid other people entirely. She stopped sitting with coworkers at lunch, stopped riding the bus with them, and instead walked two miles each way to the fields, leaving before dawn and returning after dark. She came to believe that she could not rely on herself—that she had failed to protect herself once, and would fail again. She felt like an outsider, permanently set apart from the other women who laughed and talked and seemed untouched by what she carried. The isolation was total: she was certain that no one could understand, and that if they knew, they would see her as damaged or complicit.

The threat she felt was constant. She began looking behind her frequently, checking if someone was following her, even in the grocery store or on the dirt road near her home. She came to feel safe only in a very limited number of places: her own bathroom, the corner of her living room where she could see the door, and the far end of the field where no one could approach from behind. But even there, the fear would spike, and that spike would trigger another intrusive memory—the hand, the diesel, the weight—and the cycle would begin again. Her husband noticed she was jumpy and withdrawn, but she told him she was just tired. She stopped going to church, stopped visiting her sister, stopped answering calls from her daughter. The world had become a place of threat, and she could not find a way out of it.

What finally brought Marlene to therapy was a morning when she could not get out of bed. She had been up all night, rehearsing a scenario she could not control, and she felt hollow and empty. Her daughter drove her to the clinic, and Marlene sat in the waiting room with her hands clenched, looking over her shoulder at the door. She said she did not know if talking could help. She was afraid that if she said the words out loud, the memory would become real again, and she would never escape it. But she was also afraid of what would happen if she kept going the way she was.
